newsitem.title: USA: Heart study has U.S. doctors seeking more research.
newsitem.headline: Heart study has U.S. doctors seeking more research.

text.p: A study raising doubts about a hospital procedure for investigating the condition of the heart is not strong enough evidence for doctors to change practices, the head of a physicians' group said on Wednesday.

But the recent research about right heart catheterization has prompted the medical profession to support more studies of the procedure, Bart Chernow, president of the American College of Chest Physicians (ACCP), said.

Chernow and other doctors at the ACCP's International Scientific Assembly in San Francisco held a news conference to state the ACCP's position on the study published last month in the Journal of the American Medical Association. The ACCP counts more than 16,000 chest and critical care specialists among its members.
Right heart catheterization is commonly used in hospitals to monitor critically ill patients to find out how well the heart is functioning. It has been used for 25 years.
But the observational study by U.S. researchers said right heart catheterization does patients little good and may actually increase the risk of death.

Based on the research, an editorial in the journal called for a nationwide study of right heart catheterization or, in the absence of such a study, a moratorium on the procedure by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.

"This article in and of itself does not provide strong enough evidence for physicians to change what they do ... We think that patients should not be frightened of this article coming out and should not think that physicians are doing them harm by inserting this catheter," Chernow said.
"One of the things that this article has done is to prompt us to study this issue further," he said.

After the article appeared, the ACCP appointed a blue-ribband panel of senior critical care physicians to study the issues it raised. It also polled 370 practicing critical care doctors at the San Francisco meeting Wednesday about the pulmonary artery catheters used in the procedure.

Both the panel and the doctors indicated that the journal article raised "significant questions" but did not provide enough data to warrant a change in clinical use of the catheter, the ACCP said. Panel members recommended against imposing a moratorium on use of the catheters, it said.
Chernow noted that the catheters were usually placed in sicker patients, whose health outcomes tended to be worse.
Doctors at the meeting said the recent study may make it easier to carry out the randomized trial they believe is necessary to draw firm conclusions about the procedure.

A problem with randomized studies in the past has been the need to withhold the catheter from patients in a control group, the ACCP said. Critical care physicians did not feel warranted in withholding a potentially life-saving procedure from a critically ill patient. Now, Chernow said, doctors may feel that the questions raised by the article can only be answered in a randomized study.
One such study is already under way in Canada, where the Canadian critical care trials group is doing a randomized trial on the catheter's effectiveness, Chernow said.

Dean Sandham, a professor of medicine at the University of Calgary who is leading the trial, said 1,450 patients have entered the study and researchers are aiming for 2,000 patients. The study is expected to take 20 months to complete.
